1. Scientific Analysis

Analysis Type

KPFM CPD domain analysis: volts conversion, square-pixel resampling, row-align + plane leveling, artifact masking, adaptive K-means clustering of surface potential into spatially-coherent contact-potential domains

Interpretation

The KPFM contact potential difference (CPD) map of a multi-layer hBN van der Waals stack was converted to volts, resampled to square pixels (19.53 nm/px, 10x10 um field of view), and leveled (per-row 1st-order polynomial + plane subtraction) to remove scanner drift and slow tilt. The residual stripe std after row-alignment (~2.3 mV) is small relative to the total leveled potential range (~104 mV), indicating the leveling successfully suppressed line-to-line offset artifacts without erasing the real surface-potential signal. Only 0.36% of pixels were masked as artifacts (a localized topographic/probe scarring feature in the upper-left, coincident with the bright diagonal ridge in the topography), so the clustering operated on essentially the full valid field. Adaptive K-means partitioned the leveled potential into two spatially-coherent CPD domains with mean potentials of -10.5 mV (domain 1, 35% of area) and +5.9 mV (domain 2, 65% of area), a pairwise contrast of ~16 mV. Physically, these two populations correspond to regions of differing effective work function / surface potential on the hBN surface — most plausibly areas of differing layer number (thickness terraces) or differing dielectric/charge screening, since work function in few-layer 2D materials depends on layer count and substrate coupling. The more-negative domain forms the connected diagonal band running lower-left to upper region (following the topographic terracing), while the more-positive domain occupies the broad lower-right majority. The within-domain std (~6-8 mV) is comparable to the inter-domain contrast, so the two populations are only weakly separated — consistent with the map being closer to a smooth CPD gradient than to sharply bounded discrete domains. Importantly, the domain-count selection is not robust: silhouette (0.558) and BIC (-1.558e6) both favor k=3, and only the largest-connected-component coherence criterion favors k=2. This means the true CPD landscape likely contains three (or a continuum of) potential levels, and forcing k=2 collapses a gradient into two bins. Consequently the reported ~16 mV contrast should be treated as a lower bound; the full leveled range of ~104 mV is the more honest measure of the total surface-potential heterogeneity across the flake.

3. Scientific Claims

Claim 1: The hBN surface exhibits spatially-coherent surface-potential heterogeneity with a total leveled CPD range of ~104 mV, organized into at least two work-function domains (mean CPD -10.5 mV over 35% of area vs +5.9 mV over 65% of area; pairwise contrast ~16 mV).

Scientific Impact: Spatially-correlated CPD domains in multi-layer hBN reveal layer-number- and substrate-coupling-dependent work-function variation, which governs charge injection, dielectric screening, and interfacial band alignment in vdW heterostructure devices. Mapping these domains connects local layer terracing to electrostatic potential landscape.

Literature Search Query: Has anyone observed layer-dependent contact-potential-difference domains in multi-layer hBN with inter-domain contrast on the order of tens of mV using Kelvin probe force microscopy?

Keywords: hBN, KPFM, contact potential difference, work function, van der Waals, surface potential domains

4. Caveats & Limitations

Domain-count selection is inconsistent: two of three metrics (silhouette 0.558, BIC -1.558e6) favor k=3, and k=2 was chosen only on coherence grounds, so the 2-domain partition likely under-resolves the true potential structure. Because within-domain std (~6-8 mV) is comparable to the ~16 mV inter-domain contrast, the map is closer to a smooth gradient than to discrete domains, and the reported contrast is a lower bound that under-represents the true ~104 mV range. Domain assignment to specific physical origins (layer number vs charge/screening vs contamination) is not verifiable from CPD alone without co-registered topography/thickness data. CPD absolute values are tip-work-function-referenced and not calibrated to a vacuum-level work function.
